gist: Atwood traces the Initial Principle from its hidden, negative state (the Kabalistic Unknown, Ain, divine darkness, a nothing as respects us) to its eduction into manifestation as white Light, and identifies this white, universal ground with the alchemists' Matter (vapour, salt, water that wets not, magic earth), which is 'our Identity' and is recognized only by those who have entered within to know themselves.

notes.point: Epigraph: God, alone in the beginning, created one substance, named the first matter.
Kabalah: all things psychically derived; by essential emanation the universe is corporified by multiplying the indeficient unit under the Law of its own Light.
The Zohar calls the Initial Principle Wisdom or Supreme Crown once manifest; in the Beginning, the Unknown, described negatively.

Zohar: all lay concealed in the Infinite; the Unknown manifests by producing a point, but while that point of Light stays subjective and inseparate he is unknown: Ancient of Days, White Head, Mystery of Mysteries.
Ben Jocahi: seen yet unknown, clothed in white, he shakes from his head a dew of light that awakens the dead, white as diamond, the colour containing all.
This white splendour recurs in Apocalypse and Enoch. The worldly mind deems it fanciful; only those who entered experimentally within to know themselves recognize the ground.
As colours unite in white, Nature appears white in her Fontal Light; Paracelsus: a simple ground of diversity whereon to recreate.
Lucerna Salis: the matter whitens like a hoary man, then silver; with carefully governed fire, snow-white: the white work perfected.
notes.voice: QUOTED: author of the Lucerna Salis

notes.point: Sendivogius saw and felt the Water of our Sea, not wetting the hands, white as snow.
This is the old Alchemists' Matter: an unctuous mineral vapour, into which bodies are turned; the vapour is the Stone.

It appears first in vision in demoniacal forms, known only when the purifying eye of mind meets its source, in intellectual contact with the Thing itself, our Identity. It is Orpheus's material, Cheiron's power, Silenus, Pan.
It is also Flos Salis Albi, Van Helmont's Quellum, the magic earth whose recreative fire coagulates it, the Water that wets not the hands, the Magnesia of the Mysteries.

Platonists: true Being is white. Olympiodorus: Tartarus is the soul's trial and the wholeness of existence; souls without reason follow bodily temperament, reason-ruled souls assimilate to the Supreme virtue.
The soul's first motion toward this is the true origin of matter, generative virtue allied with the medial life and light.
Reuchlin: Wisdom alone is in the beginning; retracted in darkness it is Ain, nothing as respects us; shown in human apprehension, dark Aleph becomes light Aleph.
So Paradise opened in the Seer: kindled Divine enthusiasm created the Light whence all emerge. Enoch saw the Radical Essence, Adamic Soil, the cloud before creation.

Modern Kabalists: this cloud is Divinity concentrated, birthing the primitive Ether, an attracting vacuum or understanding. Dionysius: caligo divina; Lumen de Lumine: Tenebrae activae; Parmenides: Non-being.
notes.voice: QUOTED: some modern Kabalists; Dionysius; author of the Lumen de Lumine; Parmenides

notes.point: Its End is infinite (the Oracle's precipice); nothing to consciousness before conceived, yet the only True Thing. Boehme: the first something, a darkness condensed into water, the One Thing.

method.veiled: intellectual contact of the Thing itself, which is our Identity. This is the true Hermetic material
method.plain: The Matter of the Hermetic work is the practitioner's own essential identity, met by direct intellectual contact rather than imagination.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7 says the Thing itself is 'our Identity' and that 'This is the true Hermetic material'.

also.text: this is the Matter everywhere alluded to, and so often denoted in the Mysteries
This is the true Hermetic material, which is celebrated by all is disciples

method.veiled: it is no common water, but an unctuous mineral vapour, universally subsisting
method.plain: The Matter is not ordinary water but a subtle, oily vapour present everywhere.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7: given as 'the Matter already defined so often by the old Alchemists', introduced by Atwood's rhetorical 'is not this the Matter', i.e. endorsed.
method.voice: QUOTED: the old Alchemists (endorsed by Atwood)

also.text: the Water of our Sea, the Water of Life, not wetting the hands

method.veiled: Bodies, therefore, say they, are to be turned into such a vapour, and this vapour is the Stone
method.plain: The work reduces bodies to this universal vapour; the vapour so obtained is the Stone. This chunk does not say how the reduction is done.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7 states it directly as the alchemists' rule, following their definition of the Matter.
method.voice: QUOTED: the old Alchemists (endorsed by Atwood)

method.veiled: which in demoniacal forms is at first in vision made apparent, nor known until the eye of mind, regardant and purifying, meets its First source
method.plain: The Matter first shows itself in visions of demonic forms; it is not truly known until the mind's eye, turned back and purifying itself, reaches its origin.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7 states this directly of the Matter.

method.veiled: every phantastic desire and imagination is alienated and merged in intellectual contact of the Thing itself
method.plain: The discovery is real, not a dream: fantasy and desire are left behind and absorbed into direct intellectual contact with the Thing.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7: 'the discovery of it is no dream, if we may believe the experienced; but, on the contrary...'.

also.text: the discovery of it is no dream, if we may believe the experienced

method.veiled: They only who have entered experimentally within to know themselves, have been satisfactorily able to recognize the ground
method.plain: Recognition of this ground requires experiential self-knowledge gained by turning inward, plus a faith able to tell genuine testimony from fanatical delusion.
method.basis: III.2 ¶4 directly.

also.text: they only who are gifted with an approximately faith, to discriminate their universal testimony from amongst so many fanatical delusions

method.veiled: the worldly mind is shut out from the imagination even, of occult truth
method.plain: Ordinary outward-directed consciousness cannot even imagine this truth and dismisses it as fanciful.
method.basis: III.2 ¶4; compare III.2 ¶12 on those 'chained to these exterior surfaces'.

also.text: who are chained to these exterior surfaces, content with the bare tradition of a life to come

method.veiled: all things in the hand of God are white, says the Magian, He colours them according to His pleasure
method.plain: Whiteness (all colours united) signifies the simple, undifferentiated ground underlying all diversity, on which things can be recreated without confusion.
method.basis: III.2 ¶5: Paracelsus gives as reason 'that there should be a simple ground of all diversity without confusion whereon to recreate'; prism analogy in the same paragraph.

also.text: As all colours in their prismatic unison are white, just so is the Universal Nature, described as appearing in the evolution of her Fontal Light
the aspect of this dew is white, as the diamond is white, the colour which contains all
The Platonists have declared true Being to be white

method.veiled: your matter will become white as snow. Then is your elixir perfect as to the white work
method.plain: A stage in which the matter whitens progressively (hoary, then silver, then snow-white); full whiteness marks completion of the 'white work'.
method.basis: III.2 ¶5-6 (Lucerna Salis and its verse original); Atwood links it to the white appearance of the first principle in III.2 ¶4-5.
method.voice: QUOTED: author of the Lucerna Salis (endorsed by Atwood)

also.text: he matter will become white like a hoary man, whose aged complexion resembles ice; it will also whiten more afterwards, like silver
that water was as white as snow

method.veiled: Govern your fire with a great deal of care
method.plain: The fire must be carefully regulated during the whitening. This chunk does not explain what the fire is here.
method.basis: III.2 ¶5; Latin 'Summa dilignetia ignem rege' III.2 ¶6.
method.voice: QUOTED: author of the Lucerna Salis

method.veiled: this salt is the Water that wets not the hands
method.plain: The same Matter is a 'salt' that is also a 'water' which does not wet: not an ordinary liquid. It is further named the Flower of White Salt and the Magnesia of the Mysteries.
method.basis: III.2 ¶8: 'This same, the Arabians call Flos Salis Albi'; 'this salt is the Water that wets not the hands; and that identical Magnesia'.

also.text: Flos Salis Albi --- the Flower of White Salt
that identical Magnesia that was exhibited in the Mysteries
the White Island of Vishnu; the Lord of Radha; the White Paradise

method.veiled: the white sand, Quellum, which Van Helmont speaks of as manifesting itself forth in a vivid vital soil, which spade or mattock never pierced
method.plain: The same Matter, appearing as a living soil untouched by any tool; it is the 'magic earth' in which the recreative fire dwells.
method.basis: III.2 ¶8: 'this is the white sand, Quellum'; 'This is the true magic earth wherein is the recreative fire'.

also.text: This is the true magic earth wherein is the recreative fire, even that "Land of Havilah, where good gold is"

method.veiled: this fire binds the parts thereof spontaneously to himself, coagulates them, and stops their flux
method.plain: The recreative fire within the Matter acts of itself to draw its parts together, solidify them and halt their fluidity.
method.basis: III.2 ¶8 directly.

method.veiled: that recommended by Orpheus to be taken in the cave of Mercury, and carried in both hands away
method.plain: Mythic figures are identified with the Hermetic material: what Orpheus bade be taken from the cave of Mercury, the power borne by Cheiron (cloud-begotten, from an impure ether, double, promising a more perfect life), Silenus, Pan. This chunk asserts the identities but does not explain the images.
method.basis: III.2 ¶7: 'This is the true Hermetic material ... that recommended by Orpheus'; 'this is the power borne by the Centaur Cheiron'; 'The same in Silenus'; 'this is Pan'.

also.text: this is the power borne by the Centaur Cheiron, the monster tutor of heroes, cloud-begotten, sprung from out of the nebulous impure ether, with a duplicate real, and promise of a more perfect life to come
The same in Silenus is satirically personified the most venerable preceptor of the God of Wine; and this is Pan
the foundation of the great Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will, which was once circumscribed in Intellect, for the manifestation of its Light

method.veiled: Tartarus is the place of the soul’s trial, where the balance of existence is struck, and imperfections are made manifest
method.plain: Plato's Tartarus, read ethically, is a trial of the soul in which its imperfections are exposed; read physically, it is the wholeness of existence.
method.basis: III.2 ¶9: Olympiodorus's twofold reading.

method.veiled: souls, in which reason does not preside as a charioteer, are changed according to the subject temperament of the body; but when reason has the dominion, the soul does not yield
method.plain: Without reason in control, the soul takes on the qualities of the body, as water takes those of the earth it flows through; ruled by reason, it does not yield and assimilates to the Supreme virtue.
method.basis: III.2 ¶9: Olympiodorus explicitly gives the psychical meaning of Plato's rivers and seas.

also.text: assimilated herself to the Supreme virtue

method.veiled: her first motion towards this from her ultimate artificial recessure is the true origin of matter
method.plain: The soul's first movement back toward the Supreme virtue, from its farthest withdrawal, is what these philosophers call the true origin of matter: the generative power drawn up into union with intellect and the medial life and light.
method.basis: III.2 ¶9: 'her' refers to the soul and 'this' to 'the Supreme virtue' of the preceding sentence; the clause 'when the generative virtue is drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light' specifies it. 'artificial recessure' is not explained (see ambiguities).

also.text: when the generative virtue is drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light

method.veiled: Ain, i.e., to say, Nihil quoad nos; nothing or no entity as respects us
method.plain: The hidden principle seems to be nothing only because we cannot conceive what does not appear to us, not because it is absent.
method.basis: III.2 ¶10: 'Because we, being affected with inability in the conception, do judge and imagine of those things which do not appear immediately as if they were not at all'.

also.text: it is nothing as respects the consciousness before it is conceived

method.veiled: is dark Aleph converted into light Aleph
method.plain: When the hidden principle actually shows itself in human apprehension, its darkness becomes light.
method.basis: III.2 ¶10: the conversion happens 'when it has showed itself forth to be somewhat indeed, and that it does really in the human apprehension exist'; prayer in III.2 ¶11.

also.text: Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.

method.veiled: he begins by producing a point; but, whilst the point of Light remains within subjective and inseparate, he is unknown
method.plain: Manifestation begins with a point of Light; while it stays internal and undivided the principle remains unknown, developing only by separating things within itself.
method.basis: III.2 ¶3 (Zohar, as given): 'as the Unity of things to be developed only by the separation of them in Himself'.

method.veiled: From his head he shakes a dew which awakens the dead, and brings them to new life
method.plain: A white, life-restoring 'dew of light' issues from the hidden principle; it is also the manna that nourishes the saints. This chunk links it to its theme only through whiteness and does not apply it to the practice.
method.basis: III.2 ¶3: 'Thy dew is the dew of light'; 'the manna which descends'; III.2 ¶4 follows with 'This white appearance of the primeval splendour'.

also.text: Thy dew is the dew of light

method.veiled: by that kindling of Divine enthusiasm in conjunction with its source, the soft lenient Light was created
method.plain: In the seer, the Light from which all things come arises when divine enthusiasm is kindled in union with its source; this is the opening of Paradise in him.
method.basis: III.2 ¶12 directly: 'So Paradise was opened in the Seer, and by that kindling ...'.

also.text: So Paradise was opened in the Seer

method.veiled: the wooden receptacles (the vegetable or medial life) out of which the winds became separated
method.plain: Enoch's 'wooden receptacles' mean the vegetable or medial life; with the winds, clouds and snow they belong to the Radical Essence and Adamic Soil the seer beheld.
method.basis: III.2 ¶12: the parenthetical gloss is inserted in the quotation.

also.text: what he beheld of the Radical Essence, and the manifold glories of that mystical Adamic Soil

method.veiled: This nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo before its birth
method.plain: The primordial cloud is a concentration of Divinity within its original identity, which, like a cloud before rain, gives birth to the primitive Ether.
method.basis: III.2 ¶13: 'some modern Kabalists have explained to be an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity'.

also.text: the cloud itself which continued over the earth before the creation of the world

method.veiled: the primitive Ether, which is the pure attracting vacuum, or understanding whereby the central efficient is drawn forth to will and operation
method.plain: The primitive Ether is an attracting emptiness, equivalently an understanding, which draws the central active power out into willing and acting.
method.basis: III.2 ¶13 defines it directly.

method.veiled: Dionysius styles it caligo divina, because, as he says, it is obscure and humanly incomprehensible, though visible indeed
method.plain: The originating principle is a divine or active darkness: visible yet incomprehensible, below all sense and imagination, a terrible, inexpressible chasm.
method.basis: III.2 ¶13: Dionysius and the Lumen de Lumine both describe it.
method.voice: QUOTED: Dionysius; author of the Lumen de Lumine

also.text: Tenebrae activae, and describes it as beneath all degrees of sense and imagination --- a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm

method.veiled: Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth
method.plain: A warning attached to the infinite, pre-conscious ground; with the Parmenides verse it suggests that this ground is not to be approached with ordinary mental notions. This chunk does not explain the 'precipice' (see ambiguities).
method.basis: III.2 ¶15 introduces it with 'For its End is infinite; as the Oracle forewarns' and follows with 'it is nothing as respects the consciousness before it is conceived'; III.2 ¶14: 'But there thy intellectual notions check When in this path exploring'.

also.text: But there thy intellectual notions check When in this path exploring

method.veiled: it becomes that only True Thing of which we can affirm nothing, whose theology is negative; but which constitutes the perfect possession of the most happy life
method.plain: The 'nothing' is nothing only to consciousness before it is conceived; once reached it is the one True Thing, known only negatively, and the possession of the happiest life.
method.basis: III.2 ¶15 directly, with 'it is nothing as respects the consciousness before it is conceived'.

method.veiled: this first something was a certain cloud or darkness, which was condensed into water; and this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained
method.plain: The first thing God made out of nothing was a dark cloud condensed into a water; this water is the One Thing containing all.
method.basis: III.2 ¶15 (Boehme) directly, introduced by 'This Boehme also declares'.

sources.name: Reuchlin
sources.quote: Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.
sources.use: Supports: Wisdom as Ain in darkness; dark Aleph turned to light Aleph.

sources.name: scripture ('as it is written')
sources.quote: The night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are all alike to Him
sources.use: Supports the conversion of darkness into light.

sources.name: unattributed Latin verse
sources.quote: Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.
sources.use: Illustrates darkness made light by divine illumination.

sources.name: some modern Kabalists
sources.quote: an absolute concentration of Divinity within its original identity
sources.use: Explain the nebulous apparition of the Catholic Embryo and the primitive Ether.

sources.name: Dionysius
sources.quote: caligo divina
sources.use: Supports: divine darkness, visible yet incomprehensible; the True Thing of negative theology, possession of the happiest life.

sources.name: author of the Lumen de Lumine
sources.work: Lumen de Lumine, the chapter on Matter
sources.quote: a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm
sources.use: Supports: Tenebrae activae beneath sense and imagination.

sources.name: Parmenides
sources.quote: Non-being, which nor mind can see
sources.use: Supports: Non-being is not the object of the mental eye; check intellectual notions on this path.

sources.name: the Oracle
sources.quote: Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth
sources.use: Warning about the infinite End of the principle.

sources.name: Boehme
sources.quote: this water is that One Thing in which all things are contained
sources.use: Supports: creation out of nothing of a cloud or darkness condensed into water, the One Thing.

readings: A word naming the Stone just mentioned.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: the text prints 'lais' and gives no translation. Reading 2: the phrase directly follows 'this vapour is the Stone known and proven in the Book of Life' (III.2 ¶7), with 'notus' set beside 'known'; the chunk does not confirm it.

ambiguities.quote: the foundation of the great Saturnian Monarchy of the Freed Will, which was once circumscribed in Intellect, for the manifestation of its Light
readings: The Matter (our Identity) underlies a state of freed will once contained within intellect.
'which' refers to the Matter itself (Pan), once circumscribed in Intellect.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶7: the antecedent of 'which' may be 'Monarchy' or 'Pan'/the Matter; no further explanation in the chunk.

ambiguities.quote: with a duplicate real, and promise of a more perfect life to come
readings: Cheiron's own double nature, as 'Centaur' and 'monster'.
A doubled reality of the power he bears.
ambiguities.basis: III.2 ¶7 gives no explanation; 'Centaur' and 'monster' are named just before.

readings: The soul's farthest withdrawal into body and its temperament, from which she first turns back.
A withdrawal brought about by art (an operation), from which the first motion begins.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: the preceding sentence contrasts souls changed by bodily temperament with souls assimilated to the Supreme virtue (III.2 ¶9). Reading 2: rests only on the word 'artificial', which the chunk does not explain.

ambiguities.quote: Stoop not down, for a precipice lies below in the earth
readings: A warning not to grasp the infinite ground with discursive notions.
A warning against descending toward the earthly or lower.
ambiguities.basis: Reading 1: III.2 ¶14 'But there thy intellectual notions check When in this path exploring' and III.2 ¶15 'it is nothing as respects the consciousness before it is conceived'. Reading 2: the literal image 'below in the earth'. The chunk does not gloss it.

translations.original: Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus.
translations.translation: God, when He alone was in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter.

translations.original: Omnia in Dei manu alba sunt; is eas tingit ut vult
translations.translation: all things in the hand of God are white, says the Magian, He colours them according to His pleasure

translations.original: Acquiret canitiem viri senis, Albicabitque fere ut argentums, Summa dilignetia ignem rege Videsbisque sequenter materiam in vitro Albere omnino candore nivali Et tum confectum est elixir ad album
translations.translation: he matter will become white like a hoary man, whose aged complexion resembles ice; it will also whiten more afterwards, like silver. Govern your fire with a great deal of care, and afterwards you shall see that in your vessel your matter will become white as snow. Then is your elixir perfect as to the white work.
Let the [lais] known in the chapters be taken (meaning of 'lais' not given; see ambiguities).

translations.original: Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.
translations.translation: Nothing is in the beginning but Wisdom, or Sapience.
nothing or no entity as respects us

translations.original: Tenebrae sunt ei sicut ipsa lux.
translations.translation: Darkness is to Him as the light itself. (The book sets it beside the English 'the darkness and the light are all alike to Him'.)

translations.original: Si tu, Deus meus, illuminaveris me Lux fiunt tenebrae meae.
translations.translation: If Thou, my God, enlighten me, my darkness becomes light.

threads.note: 'The Initial Principle, however, which we have been discussing' points back to the preceding discussion of the Initial Principle.
Atwood declines to enter the Method of the Kabalistic philosophy ('space does not allow us to enter'); refers readers to Rosenroth and Franck.
'Arnold, Lully, Artephius, and the rest cited in the Theory' points to an earlier section called 'the Theory' where these descriptions of whitening were cited.
'the Matter already defined so often by the old Alchemists' points back to earlier definitions of the Matter.
'The same Sendivogius' points back to an earlier mention of Sendivogius outside this chunk.
